summary.text: For \(m=39101\), let \(N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1\); modular exponentiation and gcd computations for \(2+\sqrt3\) in \((\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)[\sqrt3]\) show that, modulo every prime divisor \(p\mid N\), its order in the norm-one subgroup is divisible by \(3^{19557}\). If \(N\) were composite, its least prime divisor would satisfy \(p^2\le N\), while that subgroup has at most \(2p\) elements and a numerical bound gives \(2p<3^{19557}\), a contradiction; thus \(N\) is prime and this exponent supplies the counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 n_0=100943,
 \qquad E=2n_0\,3^{39101}=201886\,3^{39101},
 \qquad N=E-1.
\]
Thus
\[
 N=201886\,3^{39101}-1.
\]
The number \(N\) has 18662 decimal digits. We will prove that \(N\) is prime. It will then follow immediately that \(m=39101\) is a valid exponent in the definition of A354747 at \(n=100943\), disproving the assertion that the sequence value is zero.

The primality proof uses arithmetic in a quadratic algebra. For every modulus \(M\), let
\[
 A_M=(\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z)[\sqrt3].
\]
We write an element as a pair \((a,b)\), representing \(a+b\sqrt3\). Addition is coordinatewise, and multiplication is
\[
 (a,b)(c,d)=(ac+3bd,\;ad+bc)\pmod M.
\]
The identity is \((1,0)\). Define the norm by
\[
 \operatorname{Nm}(a,b)=a^2-3b^2\pmod M.
\]
A direct expansion gives
\[
 \operatorname{Nm}(uv)=\operatorname{Nm}(u)\operatorname{Nm}(v).
\]
In particular, the norm-one elements are closed under multiplication.

We use the element
\[
 x=(2,1)\in A_N.
\]
Its norm is
\[
 \operatorname{Nm}(x)=2^2-3\cdot1^2=1.
\]

Here is the finite modular computation that supplies the primality certificate. It is useful to describe it explicitly so that the certificate is reproducible using only integer arithmetic.

For pairs of integers, define
\[
 M_N((a,b),(c,d))=
 \bigl((ac+3bd)\bmod N,\;(ad+bc)\bmod N\bigr),
\]
where each remainder is the least nonnegative remainder modulo \(N\). Define
\[
 C_N(u)=M_N(M_N(u,u),u).
\]
Thus \(C_N(u)\) represents the cube of \(u\) in \(A_N\). Starting with \(u_0=(2,1)\), apply \(C_N\) successively 19556 times. The resulting pair represents
\[
 x^{3^{19556}}.
\]
Raise that pair to the power \(201886\) by ordinary binary exponentiation, using \(M_N\) for every multiplication. Call the resulting least-residue pair
\[
 z=(a,b).
\]
Consequently,
\[
 z=x^R,
 \qquad
 R=201886\,3^{19556}=\frac{E}{3^{19545}}.
\]
The exact modular exponentiation and Euclidean-algorithm calculation give
\[
 \gcd\bigl(N,\,a+N-1,\,b\bigr)=1. \tag{1}
\]
Starting from this same pair \(z\), apply \(C_N\) a further 19545 times. The result is exactly \((1,0)\). Since each application cubes the represented element, this says
\[
 z^{3^{19545}}=(1,0)\quad\text{in }A_N. \tag{2}
\]
Because \(R3^{19545}=201886\,3^{39101}=E\), equation (2) is equivalently
\[
 x^E=(1,0)\quad\text{in }A_N. \tag{3}
\]
These calculations can be organized in blocks, but no probabilistic primality test is involved: they consist solely of the displayed pair multiplication, repeated cubing, binary exponentiation, and the Euclidean algorithm. Their mathematical roles are distinct. Equation (3) puts a bound on the order of the reduction of \(x\) modulo every prime divisor of \(N\), while (1) proves that its smaller power \(x^R\) is not the identity modulo any such prime divisor.

We now establish those assertions and use them to prove primality.

Let \(p\) be any prime divisor of \(N\). Reduction of both coordinates modulo \(p\) gives a multiplicative map
\[
 A_N\longrightarrow A_p.
\]
Write \(\bar x=(2,1)\in A_p\), and similarly write \(\bar z\) for the reduction of \(z=(a,b)\). Reducing (3) modulo \(p\) gives
\[
 \bar x^E=(1,0). \tag{4}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 \bar x^R\ne(1,0). \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, suppose \(\bar x^R=(1,0)\). Since \(z=x^R\) modulo \(N\), this would imply
\[
 a\equiv1\pmod p,
 \qquad b\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Also \(p\mid N\). From \(a\equiv1\pmod p\) and \(p\mid N\), we obtain
\[
 p\mid a+N-1,
\]
and from the second congruence we obtain \(p\mid b\). Hence \(p\) divides all three integers \(N,a+N-1,b\), contradicting (1), because a prime cannot divide their gcd \(1\). This proves (5).

Consider the norm-one set
\[
 G_p=\{(u,v)\in A_p:u^2-3v^2=1\}.
\]
It is a group. Closure follows from multiplicativity of the norm; the identity belongs to it; and the inverse of \((u,v)\in G_p\) is \((u,-v)\), because
\[
 (u,v)(u,-v)=(u^2-3v^2,0)=(1,0).
\]
The element \(\bar x\) belongs to \(G_p\), since its norm is \(1\).

We need the elementary size bound
\[
 |G_p|\le 2p. \tag{6}
\]
For each fixed \(v\in\mathbb F_p\), the equation defining \(G_p\) becomes
\[
 u^2=1+3v^2.
\]
Over the field \(\mathbb F_p\), a quadratic equation \(u^2=c\) has at most two roots: if \(u^2=r^2\), then
\[
 (u-r)(u+r)=0,
\]
so \(u=r\) or \(u=-r\). Thus for each of the \(p\) possible values of \(v\), there are at most two possible values of \(u\). This proves (6). The bound also remains valid for \(p=2\), where the two possible signs may coincide.

Let \(t\) be the multiplicative order of \(\bar x\) in \(G_p\). From (4),
\[
 t\mid E. \tag{7}
\]
From (5),
\[
 t\nmid R. \tag{8}
\]
We claim that
\[
 3^{19557}\mid t. \tag{9}
\]
To see this, note first that
\[
 E=201886\,3^{39101},
 \qquad
 R=201886\,3^{19556},

a nd \(3\nmid201886\). If (9) were false, the exponent of \(3\) in the prime factorization of \(t\) would be at most \(19556\). Since \(t\mid E\), every prime factor of \(t\) other than \(3\), with its full multiplicity, must divide the factor \(201886\), while the \(3\)-part of \(t\) would divide \(3^{19556}\). It would follow that
\[
 t\mid201886\,3^{19556}=R,
\]
contradicting (8). Hence (9) holds.

As \(t>0\), (9) implies
\[
 3^{19557}\le t.
\]
The cyclic subgroup generated by \(\bar x\) has exactly \(t\) elements and is contained in \(G_p\), so (6) gives
\[
 3^{19557}\le t\le |G_p|\le2p. \tag{10}
\]
Thus every prime divisor \(p\) of \(N\) would have to satisfy \(2p\ge3^{19557}\).

We now show that this is impossible for the least prime divisor if \(N\) is composite. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(N\) is composite, and let \(p\) be its least prime divisor. Then
\[
 p^2\le N. \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, writing \(N=pq\), the cofactor \(q>1\) has a prime divisor no smaller than the least prime divisor \(p\), so \(q\ge p\).

We next prove
\[
 2p<3^{19557}. \tag{12}
\]
The small numerical inequality
\[
 4\cdot201886=807544<3^{13}=1594323
\]
combined with \(N=201886\,3^{39101}-1\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
4N
&=4(201886\,3^{39101}-1)\\
&<4\cdot201886\,3^{39101}\\
&<3^{13}3^{39101}\\
&=3^{39114}\\
&=(3^{19557})^2.
\end{aligned} \tag{13}
\]
By (11),
\[
 (2p)^2=4p^2\le4N.
\]
Together with (13), this yields
\[
 (2p)^2<(3^{19557})^2.
\]
Both sides being positive, (12) follows.

But (12) contradicts (10). Therefore \(N\) cannot be composite. Since \(N>1\), it is prime.

We have proved, explicitly, that
\[
 2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1=N

a
\]
is prime. Also \(39101>0\). Therefore \(39101\) belongs to the set
\[
 S=\{m\in\mathbb N:m\ge1\text{ and }2\cdot100943\cdot3^m-1\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
In particular, \(S\) is nonempty. Every member of \(S\) is positive, so its least member is positive; indeed it lies between \(1\) and \(39101\). By the definition of A354747, this least member is \(a(100943)\). Consequently
\[
 a(100943)\ne0.
\]
Thus the conjecture \(a(100943)=0\) is false; the exponent \(m=39101\) supplies a counterexample.
